name: YK-11
lead: YK-11 is a synthetic steroidal compound sold online as a muscle-building product, and in appearance terms it is discussed for one reason: people take an interest in it as a route to a more muscular, fuller physique. It is usually classed as a selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). Wikipedia describes it as a gene-selective partial agonist of the androgen receptor that does not trigger the N/C interaction normally needed for full receptor activation, with anabolic activity in cultured C2C12 myoblasts greater than that of dihydrotestosterone (DHT).[1]

The compound was reported by Yuichiro Kanno and colleagues at Toho University, Japan, around 2011, and a 2013 paper in Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin reported that YK-11 raised follistatin expression in myoblasts, the basis of its marketing as a myostatin inhibitor.[2][3][31] Published work consists of cell and animal studies, including a 2021 mouse sepsis study and a 2018 osteoblast cell study; no human clinical trial of YK-11 was found.[1][31]

The rationale people give is a chain: partial androgen receptor activation, higher follistatin, less active myostatin, and so more muscle growth. Myostatin is a protein that limits muscle size, and follistatin is one of the proteins that binds it, which is why the pathway attracts interest in bodybuilding.[29][30] Researchers describe the YK-11 link to this pathway as shown in cultured cells, not in people.[31]

YK-11 is not authorised as a medicine anywhere noted in the sources. Health Canada warned in 2022 that SARMs such as YK-11 are not authorised for any use and that bodybuilding products containing them can pose risks such as heart attack, stroke and liver damage.[1] It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list and has been detected in doping control samples and in dietary supplements.[2][5][6]

sections.h: Background: SARMs and the myostatin pathway
paras: SARMs are compounds designed to activate the androgen receptor in muscle and bone while having less effect on tissues such as the prostate. According to Wikipedia, the first non-steroidal SARMs were developed independently in 1998 by groups at the University of Tennessee and at Ligand Pharmaceuticals, and the term was introduced in 1999. As of 2023 no SARM had been approved by the US FDA or the European Medicines Agency.[28] Candidates such as enobosarm (ostarine) and LGD-4033 (ligandrol) reached clinical trials; a phase III enobosarm trial raised lean body mass without a significant improvement in physical function.[28] YK-11 sits outside that development pipeline: it was characterised in an academic laboratory and has not entered clinical development.[1][28]

Myostatin (GDF-8) limits skeletal muscle growth. Its discovery is credited to Se-Jin Lee and Alexandra McPherron, whose 1997 knockout mice had roughly twice the normal muscle mass, and naturally occurring myostatin mutations explain the double-muscled Belgian Blue and Piedmontese cattle. A German boy with mutations in both copies of the gene, reported in 2004, was noticeably stronger than his peers.[30] Follistatin binds and neutralises activin and myostatin; Lee and McPherron reported in 2001 that blocking myostatin or raising follistatin increased muscle mass in mice.[29] Wikipedia notes that as of 2012 no myostatin inhibitor had been approved for humans, and that long-term use in muscular dystrophy is uncertain.[30] Bodybuilding discussion of YK-11 borrows from this literature when it calls the compound a myostatin inhibitor.

YK-11 has no approved medical use. Wikipedia notes animal investigation for sepsis-induced muscle wasting.[1] It is sold by online vendors as a research chemical and bodybuilding product, sometimes labelled myostine, and sometimes touted in bodybuilding circles as a potent myostatin inhibitor even though it remains experimental.[1][2] T Nation posters have described cycles with it alone or alongside other SARMs, GW501516 and andarine, and a mix that dropped RAD-140 for YK-11 and andarine.[7][8][9]

No studies found. No human clinical trial of YK-11 has been published.[1] The related SARM class has human data: randomised trials of other SARMs report lean body mass gains in the range of about 1 to 1.5 kg alongside suppression of testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin and HDL cholesterol, according to a 2026 review in Drug Testing and Analysis, but those results concern other compounds and cannot be transferred to YK-11.[32] A published case report documented detection of YK-11 in an athlete's doping control sample, which is an analytic finding and not a treatment study.[10]

In the 2013 Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin paper, Kanno and colleagues treated C2C12 mouse myoblasts with YK-11 and found stronger induction of myogenic differentiation than with DHT, with higher expression of the myogenic regulatory factors MyoD, Myf5 and myogenin. Unlike DHT, YK-11 induced follistatin expression, and an anti-follistatin antibody reversed the differentiation effect, which the authors took to mean follistatin mediates the anabolic action.[3][31]

A 2018 study from the same Toho University group (Yatsu and colleagues, with Kanno) used MC3T3-E1 mouse osteoblast cells. YK-11 and DHT both accelerated proliferation and mineralisation, YK-11 increased the differentiation markers osteoprotegerin and osteocalcin, and an androgen receptor blocker prevented the effects. YK-11 also increased phosphorylated Akt, which the authors read as rapid non-genomic receptor signalling.[12][31]

Lee and colleagues (Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications, 2021) gave YK-11 to mice infected with gram-negative bacteria. Sepsis raised muscle myostatin; YK-11 was reported to inhibit myostatin, lower pro-inflammatory cytokines and organ-damage markers and reduce mortality. The authors suggested YK-11 might help reverse sepsis-related muscle wasting.[27][31]

Dahleh and colleagues (Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, 2023) reported that in male Wistar rats treated for five weeks, YK-11 increased oxidative stress and disrupted the antioxidant system and mitochondrial function markers in the hippocampus. Swimming exercise alone was neuroprotective; combining exercise with YK-11 prevented some, but not all, of the changes.[13][31]

Kanno's group found that YK-11 activates the androgen receptor as a partial agonist, promoting nuclear translocation without inducing the amino/carboxyl-terminal interaction that DHT induces.[1][2] In C2C12 myoblasts, YK-11 promoted myogenic differentiation more strongly than DHT, with the 2013 paper attributing this to increased expression of follistatin, a protein that binds and neutralises myostatin, a negative regulator of muscle mass.[3][2] A later cell study reported that YK11 up-regulates additional factors in cultured cells, and a 2023 paper reported that YK11 induced oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, which Grokipedia describes as occurring in the hippocampus.[12][13][2] These are laboratory findings and have not been shown in humans.

Grokipedia adds that YK-11 enhances osteoblast differentiation and Akt signalling in cell lines, and its chemical name describes a 19-norpregnane backbone, which is why some forum users and commentators say it resembles a steroid more than a non-steroidal SARM.[2][14][15]

Wikipedia cites a March 2021 paper in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications (Lee and colleagues) describing YK11 as a myostatin inhibitor for preventative use against bacterial sepsis in animal work; the paper's findings concern animals, not people.[27]

Wikipedia describes the receptor behaviour as gene-selective partial agonism: YK-11 binds the androgen receptor and drives some genes without the full N/C interaction, which is cited as one reason its effects in cells differ from those of DHT.[1] Wikipedia's SARM article says the mechanism of tissue selectivity in the class remains debated, with proposals including lack of conversion by 5-alpha-reductase and differential recruitment of coactivators and corepressors.[28]

Most pharmacokinetic work is from anti-doping research: mass spectrometric characterisation, equine metabolism after oral dosing (which detected the parent compound and phase I metabolites in plasma and urine) and detection in horse mane hair.[16][17][18] A validation study screening 60 dietary supplements purchased online in 2020 found undisclosed MK-677 and YK-11 in some products.[19]

Human safety data for YK-11 are absent. Health Canada states that SARM-containing bodybuilding products can pose serious risks including heart attack, stroke and liver damage, and that long-term effects are unknown.[1] One forum poster, replying to a user with health problems after SARMs, said YK-11's structure resembles an oral methylated steroid, and another poster reported side effects from a cycle that he said outweighed the modest results.[20][24]

For the SARM class, Wikipedia reports that clinical trials of pharmaceutical candidates found mild and infrequent adverse events, with raised liver enzymes, lowered HDL cholesterol and dose-dependent suppression of testosterone; it also lists several case reports linking recreational SARM use to drug-induced liver injury and states that cardiovascular risk is unknown.[28] Recent case reports describe cholestatic or hepatocellular liver injury after products containing RAD-140, andarine, LGD-4033, ostarine and other SARMs, including a 2025 report described as the first adolescent case; these concern other compounds sold in similar products.[32] A 2026 review reports that the main serious harm in the class is cholestatic liver injury, usually reversible.[32]

YK-11 is a steroidal compound: according to Grokipedia, its chemical name is (17alpha,20E)-17,20-[(1-methoxyethylidene)bis(oxy)]-3-oxo-19-norpregna-4,20-diene-21-carboxylic acid methyl ester, molecular formula C25H34O6, with a molecular weight of about 430.5. Its orthoester group can hydrolyse in acid.[2] Grokipedia is AI-generated and was used only for these structural details, which should be checked against primary chemistry sources.

Most pharmacokinetic work on YK-11 comes from anti-doping laboratories: mass spectrometric characterisation in 2017, equine metabolism work, and detection in horse mane hair.[16][17][18] A 2020 screen of 60 dietary supplements purchased online found undisclosed MK-677 and YK-11 in some products.[19] A 2026 review states that only about half of products sold as SARMs contained a SARM in one analysis, and reports that WADA adverse analytical findings for the class rose from 15 in 2014 to 142 in 2019 before falling to 106 in 2024.[32] Wikipedia notes SARMs are banned by WADA since 2008, and that products sold as SARMs sometimes contain other agents such as ibutamoren or GW501516.[28]

YK-11 was reported in 2011 by Kanno and colleagues, with a 2013 Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin paper on follistatin expression and myogenic differentiation.[2][3] The 2018 osteoblast study extended the Toho group's work to bone cells, and a 2021 mouse study proposed a use in sepsis.[12][27] Detection of the compound in doping samples and in supplements followed, with analytical papers appearing from 2017 onwards.[10][16][19] In 2022 Health Canada named YK-11 (myostine) in a warning.[1]

Health Canada issued a 2022 warning naming YK-11 (myostine), and WADA lists SARMs as prohibited at all times.[1][5] The anti-doping literature includes a 2024 letter on detection of YK-11 in a doping control sample.[10] Wikipedia notes that marketing SARMs for human consumption is illegal in some jurisdictions, that Australia classifies them as prescription-only (Schedule 4) and that criminal convictions have occurred in the United States for selling them for human use.[28] SARMs are often sold as research chemicals labelled as not for human consumption.[28]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, YK-11 is described as an untested SARM of steroid-like structure, a compound with serious potential, or a compound that did nothing for the poster; one participant said it did not give notable results and outweighed the side effects.[20][21][22][23][24] Another poster said a friend uses it because it shares a base structure with DHT, and a poster asked whether it is acceptable to combine every SARM including untested ones.[25][26]

lore.intro: YK-11 is discussed on forums as a steroid-like SARM that supposedly acts as a myostatin inhibitor, with mixed user reports.[22][23][24]

claims.claim: YK-11 is a myostatin inhibitor that builds muscle beyond ordinary SARMs
claims.believers: Posters cite its follistatin-raising result in cells and describe it as having serious potential.[22][23]
claims.experts: The follistatin finding comes from cultured mouse myoblasts; no human study has tested YK-11, and Wikipedia describes it only as an investigational partial agonist.[3][1]

claims.claim: YK-11 is really a steroid, not a SARM
claims.believers: Users note its structure resembles an oral methylated steroid or has a DHT-like base.[20][21][25]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia both describe it as a steroidal SARM and a gene-selective partial agonist.[1][2]

claims.believers: One user said a cycle gave okay results; another said it did nothing.[24][21]

claims.claim: All SARMs, including YK-11, can be safely stacked
claims.believers: A poster argued that mild suppression seen with one SARM implies safety in combining all SARMs.[25]
claims.experts: Health Canada says the long-term effects of SARM products are unknown.[1]

claims.claim: Products sold as YK-11 are what they say they are
claims.believers: Some posters buy from supplement shops and rely on the owner.[26]
claims.experts: A supplement analysis found YK-11 present undisclosed in some products, so contents can differ from labels.[19]

claims.claim: YK-11 raises follistatin, so it works like a myostatin inhibitor
claims.believers: Posters cite the follistatin result and the myostatin-inhibitor label used by vendors.[22][23]
claims.experts: The follistatin result was seen in mouse myoblasts and a mouse sepsis model; no human data exist.[31][1]

claims.claim: SARMs are a safe alternative to steroids
claims.believers: Some T Nation threads discuss SARMs as a milder route than steroids and argue that mild suppression means stacking is acceptable.[8][25]
claims.experts: Reviews describe liver injury case reports and suppression of testosterone and HDL cholesterol in the class; Health Canada lists heart attack, stroke and liver damage as risks.[1][28][32]

angle.text: YK-11 is sold as a muscle-building SARM and marketed as a myostatin inhibitor. The muscle link comes from cell-culture findings in myoblasts rather than any human data.
